item.title: Resistance Isn’t a Human Flaw, It’s a Feature
item.description:
Procrastination

Resistance Isn’t a Human Flaw, It’s a Feature

Could procrastination, writer’s block, and resistance be signals of human care?

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Writer's block and procrastination may be important signals, not character flaws.
  • Resistance shows up hardest exactly when the work matters most.
  • AI never experiences this, and that absence of humanity is a sign, not an advantage.
Source: Lisa Rothstein

I’ve watched four YouTube videos, done a load of laundry, and scored some amazing deals online, getting ready to write this post. Or I might say, avoiding writing this post.

So, I put it off for longer than necessary. The idea was formed and the cartoon got drawn weeks ago, but for writing, I felt too restless to sit, and too uncomfortable confronting this very issue that so many creative people face every single day.

These days, it can be really tempting to use AI to just skip not so much the work but the creative heebie-jeebies, the acute discomfort and restlessness, the overwhelming reluctance to just... start already.

Now, I’ll be honest and say I will happily—even gleefully—offload impossibly tedious or repetitive admin work like writing proposals and “just-the-facts-ma’am” emails to my committees to my bestie Claude. Those tasks neither require nor deserve anything special or specific to me, which is probably the main reason why I find them so crushingly boring.

But when it comes to anything remotely creative or expressive, I know in my bones that the easy, beguiling off-ramp AI offers is so dangerous. Not just because I imagine all our brains becoming atrophied and melting to goo from lack of use, but because ignoring and bypassing this discomfort is like running a 5K on a broken ankle because you found some really good painkillers, or relying on a bottle of vodka every time you need to step on a stage.

This Means War

In his excellent book The War of Art, novelist and screenwriter Stephen Pressfield calls it Resistance. Note the capital R, because in his framing, it’s not just a condition or a feeling; it’s a living entity and an enemy, practically tangible and real enough to merit a proper name.

He talks about doing battle with Resistance every day, right down to his mud-and-blood combat descriptions. (I told you it was painful!)

But while being a fearsome adversary, Resistance can also be a dependable sign that you, as a human and not a robot, actually care about what you’re avoiding working on.

And the more the work matters, says Pressfield, the tougher and sneakier Resistance gets.

AI, conveniently, never has writer’s block. You can ask it to do something you'd have avoided for days or weeks, and taken almost as long to complete (conjure up a description of your ideal client, create your business plan, write a poem, a song, or a piece like this one) and have a serviceable draft in about 20 seconds.

You might think that’s because it has all the thoughts and information ever generated at its instantaneous disposal, and you’d be right. But only partly.

Claude’s biggest edge over me when it comes to licking Resistance is that he (she?) is not me. Claude doesn’t care what others think, or wonder if deep down he has anything worthwhile to impart to anyone. He’s not picking apart the wash technique on his latest cartoon, or looking for ways to express what’s in his heart. He’s not trying to connect.

Only you and I can do that. And we must.

So how might we do battle with Resistance, and win? Fortunately, science offers some clues.

Deconstructing and Foiling Resistance

Ahmed and Güss's 2022 study of writer’s block showed it wasn't just one thing. The researchers who studied 146 writers found blocking rarely comes down to laziness; it's most often driven by stress, fear of judgment, or simple exhaustion.

Of the solutions the subjects found, one was simply white-knuckling and forcing themselves to write anyway, while gentler approaches that helped most included talking over their ideas with others, switching to a different writing project, or just taking a break.

For me, just the idea that Resistance is proof I’m a human who cares, not an insurmountable barrier, a character flaw, or reason to quit gives me a reframe that helps me get started and stick with it. Then I find it almost as hard to stop.

And it’s not just me: Alice Flaherty, a neurologist at Harvard Medical School and author of The Midnight Disease: The Drive to Write, Writer's Block, and the Creative Brain, frames writer's block and its opposite (compulsive, uncontrollable writing, aka hypergraphia) as two sides of one brain-level phenomenon.

Seeing Resistance (and hypergraphia, its mirror-image) as a physiological event in the brain, rather than something to reproach ourselves for, gives us options that the usual self-help, productivity, and willpower advice can’t. Instead of staring at the blank page, questioning your self-worth and further roiling your stress hormones, you can trick your brain into a calmer, more creative flow by switching to a lower-stakes task like freewriting, or rejiggering your dopamine levels with even small changes in light or movement.

Don't Let the Creator and the Critic Share an Office

Also, no matter what the activity, I have to keep reminding myself: it’s important to separate the purely creative function from the critical, or editing, mode. Trying to edit as you write may seem efficient but it only encourages the kind of perfectionism that has you second-guessing yourself every other word or brushstroke.

That’s why, in innovation sessions, we alternate between the divergent (idea generation) and convergent (narrowing down the ideas) and don’t try to do both at once, like hitting the accelerator and brake at the same time.

Not only is mixing these two functions counterproductive, but it makes creative work a lot less fun. (As if we needed yet another reason to avoid doing it!)

So if you’re feeling stuck, blocked, or like doing laundry right now is of utmost importance instead of creating something that matters, congratulations! You are a human being. Instead of wishing that away, learn to do battle with it, as Stephen Pressfield says. Or better yet, make friends with it.

item.title: Research Shows Diet/Exercise Tracking Has Minimal Effects
item.description:
Diet

Research Shows Diet/Exercise Tracking Has Minimal Effects

Behavioral self-monitoring shows little benefit, according to 20 years of data.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Numerous systematic reviews and meta-analyses synthesize findings from hundreds of studies over 20-plus years.
  • The most meaningful changes from tracking diet and/or exercise are found in daily step-count increases.
  • Presentations of the evidence sometimes overstate the real-world significance of their findings.

So far in this series, we’ve looked at the new ubiquity of numerical measures in body-related matters, and we’ve considered a cultural-evolution argument for why they may have spread so successfully regardless of benefits.

Now we turn to the question of evidence. What systematic evidence is there to suggest that keeping numerical track of things like energy input (eating) and energy output (exercise) has beneficial effects? The benefits might involve positive changes to those variables themselves, and/or changes in bodyweight or body composition, blood pressure, cholesterol, pain, or other quality-of-life factors. Once we’ve surveyed the benefits, we can ask how they stack up against the harms.

A note on the link with eating disorders and disordered eating: For now, I’ll be taking claims of benefits at face value. If a study is trying to help increase physical activity or reduce body weight, I’ll be assessing whether it succeeds in helping people do that. But later parts of the series will go deeper, for it is not necessarily the case that everyone who thinks (or has been told) that they should eat less or be more physically active will benefit from taking more steps or ingesting fewer calories. The difference between what humans actually need and what numerical tools allow them to achieve is at the heart of what’s interesting in all this. So for now, please remember that when I say that something “helped” or “worked,” I mean merely that it did what it was intended to.

Overview of Research on Tracking Diet and Exercise

There’s no shortage of experimental evidence trying to answer the question “does tracking diet and exercise improve health?” In an informal search, I found 14 systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and umbrella analyses, collectively analysing hundreds of individual studies conducted over decades. Doubtless I could have found a 15th if I’d kept looking, but the patterns that emerge from these 14 are clear enough that I feel confident predicting that more examples wouldn’t radically change the picture.

And what is that picture? Well, in a nutshell: tracking helps a bit. It does not work wonders. It often encourages change in the intended direction, but usually only weakly.

Let’s get more specific. Here are eight simple takeaways from my reading of the state of the evidence about food and movement tracking and health.

  1. The clearest “beneficial” changes are to daily step count, which was found to increase by between 475 and 2,592 steps a day. (e.g., Kirk et al., 2019; Laranjo et al., 2021; Brickwood et al., 2019; Larsen et al., 2022)
  2. Weight loss is minimal, with effects varying from no change to a maximum of 2.87 kg for trials lasting up to 12 months. (e.g., Flores Mateo et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2020; Berry et al., 2021; Chew et al., 2022)
  3. Tracking works better when combined with other support and individually tailored, i.e., it is not a magic bullet. Tailoring might mean that a device provides different messages based on individual characteristics; additional support might involve text messaging, biofeedback, professional input or “human counselling” via phone or video call, or even an entire “comprehensive weight-loss program." (e.g., Cheatham et al., 2018; Brickwood et al., 2019; Laranjo et al., 2021; Vetrovsky et al., 2022; Lech et al., 2026)
  4. Tracking may not work for young people (Cheatham et al., 2018) or old people (80+). (Liu et al., 2020)
  5. Effects on “downstream” measures—i.e., things that we might expect to be affected by changes in diet and exercise, like systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, LDL cholesterol concentration—are weak and/or not widely studied. For example, Ferguson et al.’s (2022) “systematic review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses” focused on improvements to health concludes that “Effects for other physiological (blood pressure, cholesterol, and glycosylated haemoglobin) and psychosocial (quality of life and pain) outcomes were typically small and often non-significant.”
  6. Inquiries into more experiential matters are even scarcer, though the ones that do exist show some promise for pain and physical ability: Ferguson et al. (2022) note that out of 39 reviews and meta-analyses identified, “Only seven meta-analyses addressed psychosocial outcomes, finding small effect sizes for quality of life, whereas those for pain and disability were moderate."
  7. Statistically significant isn’t the same as real-world significant. In Berry et al. (2021), for example, the mean weight loss of 2.87 kg across 12 included studies lasting between three and 12 months is presented as “suggesting meaningful and clinically significant effect of behavioral self-monitoring on reducing obesity-related morbidity and mortality.” But anyone at risk from bodyfat-related disease is, I imagine, unlikely to benefit from losing less than 3 kilos. (The composition of the lost weight is also never reported, and is unlikely to have been all fat.) Similarly, Ferguson et al.’s (2022) discussion of effect sizes tries to present weight loss as an exception to the general rule of non-significant change: “weight-loss outcomes […] showed moderate effects, equating to a reduction in weight of about 1 kg or in BMI of 0·5 kg/m2, and a reduction of 1·5 cm in waist circumference." Again, 1.5 cm around the waist isn’t nothing, but 1 kg is more or less nothing. (And suspiciously, for 1 kg to equate to half a BMI point, an individual would have to be considerably shorter than 5-foot.) Further downstream, the changes reported by Chew et al. (2022) and Franssen et al. (2020) to blood pressure and cholesterol can be considered minor fluctuations at the individual level, even though they claim “beneficial effects on important health-related outcomes.”
  8. Authors may be more actively misleading in claiming real-world significance. Berry et al., for instance, say that “Weight loss of at least 0.5 kg has been associated with 54% lower risk of overall mortality,” but the reference cited in support (Agha & Agha, 2017a, 2017b) makes no mention of anything compatible with it. The briefest sanity check also suggests that it’s nonsense: Anyone’s weight can easily fluctuate by far more than half a kilo day to day. A quick online search for “0.5 kg and 54% mortality risk” yielded an unrelated study finding a 54% reduction in mortality from a shift from the “obese” BMI range in early adulthood to the “overweight” range in midlife (Xie et al., 2020), i.e., from far greater changes than a mere half-kilo. In a juicy numerical irony, the other study that popped up for me (Zhang et al., 2025) found that losing more than 10 kg could actually increase all-cause mortality. The same structure of “mistake” can be found in Ferguson et al.’s (2022) discussion of what counts as real-world significance with physical activity: “In public health terms, an increase of 5-10 min per day of MVPA is generally considered meaningful, suggesting the degree of change seen in this umbrella review is clinically significant.” Again, the cited reference makes no mention of the figures given here: Kraus et al. (2019) discuss associations between absolute amounts of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (e.g., minutes per week) and cardiovascular disease, but nowhere do they state that a tiny daily increase is meaningful to health.

Limited Real-World Benefits

In sum, the picture is pretty uninspiring—or, depending on your perspective, heartening. If you wear a movement tracker and monitor what you eat, you may end up taking more steps or losing a small amount of weight, especially if you also have plenty of other support that isn’t the tracking itself, but nothing else is likely to change. Given my skepticism about quantification of bodily things, you might worry that I’m not unbiased in this interpretation. But I was expecting, embarking on this overview of the evidence, that the argument I would end up making would be something like “Tracking gives us objective health benefits but may also have neglected downsides.” As it turns out, the objective health benefits are themselves minimal.

item.title: Basking in Reflective Glory and the Pronouns “We” and “They”
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Basking in Reflective Glory and the Pronouns “We” and “They”

The language of fandom shapes our identity and helps us find ourselves.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Fans share in team success by saying "we," even if not actively playing.
  • Pronouns shift from "we" to "they" when fans feel let down by losses.
  • The opposite of pride is not humility for sports fans; it is shame.
Loyal fans celebrate stellar performance by wearing their favorite players’ jerseys.
Source: Josh Allen, number 17, photo courtesy Eric Drost via Wikimedia Commons (2018).

In my hometown, at a wedding or a funeral, you will not see people dressed in a blue jersey with the number 17 sewn on the front.

But it seems like just about everywhere else—at sports bars, of course, but also at the supermarket, in the neighborhood, even at the office on “casual Fridays”—fans are honoring the Buffalo Bills quarterback, Josh Allen. Meanwhile, admirers are joining his fame, celebrating his stellar performances, and together with one voice, cheering his prospects. It says so on the pullover, the hoodie, the t-shirt, and the coffee mug.

As it happens so far early in this season, “we” are winning, spectacularly.

"We"

I use the pronoun advisedly. Fifty years ago, a young psychologist, Robert B. Cialdini, and his colleagues noticed a very interesting phenomenon when they conducted field experiments into fans’ emotions.

They found that people tended to personally associate themselves with a team’s success even though they had nothing, per se, to do with it. (Perhaps the loud “home-field advantage” is a possible exception as the 13th Man drowns out the opposing quarterback’s calls.) However, no spectator at an NFL game gets to throw a touchdown pass; nobody sitting in the stadium will leap for that game-changing interception. (Though spectators will sympathize deeply and with heart, feeling the vibe, mirror neurons firing.) And nobody watching at home can expect that their team will hear their gleeful shouts and favorable murmurs. Still, devotees proudly and personally bask in the glow of their team’s victories.

With loyalty rewarded, Monday mornings after a hometown victory are noticeably bouncier; We looked good on offense, didn’t we? Our defense flawlessly coordinated the blitz and the coverage. We stayed tough on third-down plays. After Cialdini noted this tendency, sports psychologists have anagrammed the enthusiasm BIRG-ing. BIRG-ing is the act of “basking in reflective glory.”

Basking in reflective glory is something like getting a suntan. The task may seem active and even purposeful, but you’re really just lying there, soaking in the light of “we’re number one.”

Testing BIRG-ing

A half-century ago, the team of psychologists set out to test and demonstrate the BIRG-ing phenomenon in three ways. The first looked at how often university students wore apparel that identified their school by name. Understandably, when their teams were winning, school’s sweatshirts appeared more often on the student body than when teams were losing. Especially on Mondays after a game. So much is unsurprising and plain to see.

The second and third field trials, however, yielded subtler and more interesting results. Students whose team had been victorious, the researchers noted, tended more often to personalize their team and identify with it, using the first-person plural. When students said “we” referring to their victorious team, the researchers concluded, they proclaimed a wish to “enhance one’s public image” as a reflection of the team’s success, that is. When they said “we,” they meant “they,” of course, but they said “we” as if they, themselves, had managed the victory.

And that kind of basking, the sharing of and taking credit for, is a little bit funny. Because, once again, however much we viewers strain sympathetically and positively from the safety of the couch or the recliner, professionals down on the field are doing the tush-push for a touchdown. A “simple affiliation,” the researchers concluded, proved sufficient impetus to “trumpet” success and “publish” the swelling pride. (Yes, swelling pride might well edge over into gloating.) And so we see proof of the sentiment on fans’ buttons, bumper stickers, yard signs, and inflatable buffalos that light up at night.

The "Good" in Good Feelings

It is easy to list the dividends of these good feelings. Common admiration draws a community together in shared devotion. As malign forces elsewhere work to profit by dividing and isolating us, the game stakes out a non-partisan circle of spirit that gathers us and bolsters us. Families, too, even if far-flung, will tune into the big game back home and share FaceTime commentary at halftime. And then the soul of competition itself, the drive to excel in a dangerous game, provides object lessons in resilience, strength, and persistence.

Fans in this town can weather a loss on the field or a lake-effect whiteout. When fans say, “Go Bills!” they sometimes mean “We’re hanging in there.”

Togetherness

Sociologist and play theorist Thomas Henricks describes the feeling of equalizing togetherness as communitas. Finding a common commitment and a central shared passion, Henricks argues, is one way we find our selves, individually. Losing ourselves in the game, de-individualizing, helps us find where we belong. In the context of sport, this feeling of communitas is temporary and event-driven without becoming ephemeral because it is likely to recur as celebrants gather. The crowds will be back at the stadium; the fan clubs will once again convene. Finding where they belong puts them in a generous mood.

When "We" Becomes "They"

Some loyal fan bases remain extraordinarily generous and patient. Win or lose, game after game, the Cleveland Browns packed its end zone with body-painted followers who called themselves the Dog Pound. With the memory of four consecutive unsuccessful Super Bowl appearances still fresh, the Buffalo Bills retained the loyalty of their steadfast fans, despite failing to reach the playoffs for 17 successive seasons. But elsewhere, in Los Angeles, Miami, and Phoenix, sub .500 seasons promptly resulted in sparsely attended games.

Sports psychologists have labeled the phenomenon opposite to BIRG-ing. They call it CORF-ing, “cutting off reflective failure.” Former or fair-weather fans will distance themselves from a losing team so as not to be put in a bad light. The yard signs come down, the team jersey goes back in the dresser, and the team-themed buttons end up in the junk drawer alongside unlabeled keys and expired coupons.

Tellingly, it turns out, disgruntled fans change their pronoun choice when their team suffers a prolonged drought. We becomes They. They lost. They couldn’t convert the third downs. They could not defend against the pass rush. They could not avoid costly penalties. They fumbled the ball. Generosity and forbearance drain away. We have not failed, but they, those chokers, surely have.

And this makes sense. After all, self-esteem lies at stake, and the opposite of pride is not humility for fans; it is shame.
